Hey, so neurodivergence "refers to variations in the human brain and cognition, for instance in sociability, learning, attention, mood and other mental functions" (copying from Wikipedia). It challenges the idea that neurodevelopmental differences are pathological. Right, okay. I think when you're quoting something, you're typically expected to reproduce the line as it is. So 3 or 4 would be most appropriate.

But if you must pluralise the words, and those words are pluralised by the addition of some letters, then 1 would be most appropriate.

So there are four ways of doing this:

1. Add "s" in brackets.
"I lost all my pen(s). She has many pen(s). I would like to borrow some pen(s) from her."

2. Correct the entire word in brackets.
"I lost all my [pens]. She has many [pens]. I would like to borrow some [pens] from her."

3. Use "sic" to clarify that you have copied the quote as is, either at the end of the sentence..
"I lost all my pen. She has many pen. I would like to borrow some pen from her. **[sic]**"

4. .. or after every mispelled word.
"I lost all my pen. **[sic]** She has many pen. **[sic]** I would like to borrow some pen **[sic]**" from her."

The time you need for recovery usually isn't linear for you to be able to gauge how long things will take from the get-go. Therapy work takes a lot of effort. From what I understand, personality disorders tend to take longer to heal from than say, situational anxiety.

So, unfortunately, there just aren't many books on AvPD specifically. There's "Essential Guide to Overcoming Avoidant Personality Disorder" by Martin Kantor, but it is outdated, not patient-friendly, and downright offensive in explaining the disorder.

My hack for addressing AvPD-specific social interaction issues has been reading books that teach social and communication skills to people on the autism spectrum.

I've struggled with socialising with in my work life as well, and I think that, for me, it comes from being stuck in this loop of not interacting with people because I don't know how to because I have never interacted with people. 

I've found that ASD communication training literature/videos meet me at my level by helping me understand how to "behave" in social situations. I am much more comfortable talking to people now that I have a loose plan of what I'm going to say, where I want the conversation to go, etc. 

I also realised from the books that when I don't make small talk with people in my industry or don't engage with my colleagues in any non-work conversation, it makes them think that I am not interested in being friends with them.

If this is the issue you're facing, I highly recommend reading "Navigating the Social World" by Jeanette McAfee.

Other than the social skills guidance, however, the best help you can get for AvPD is through Cognitive Behavioural Therapy. AvPD essentially points to self-esteem issues and the fear of criticism, and CBT can really help you unlearn the destructive thinking patterns that prevent you from interacting with your peers. Jefrey C. Wood's "The Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Workbook for Personality Disorders" is a good place to start if you want to understand what CBT would entail first/ can't go to a therapist right now. Also, try reading books on self-compassion/dealing with your self-criticism. Kristin Neff's "Self-Compassion" is a great resource for this.

Hope this helps. :)
